content: Chagas disease, also known as American trypanosomiasis, is an infectious disease caused by the flagellate protozoan parasite Trypanosoma cruzi (T. cruzi). Globally, it is estimated that 5 to 8 million individuals are infected, with an incidence rate of approximately 100 to 400 cases per 100,000 people. The majority of cases are reported in South America, where it is considered the most common parasitic infection. The primary mode of transmission is vector-borne, occurring through exposure to the feces or urine of infected triatomine insects (commonly known as kissing bugs). The incubation period for T. cruzi is typically 1 to 2 weeks following transmission. During the acute phase of infection, 90% to 95% of individuals remain asymptomatic. However, most patients remain chronically infected, with clinical manifestations often appearing several years or even decades after the initial infection. Approximately one-third of patients develop chronic Chagas disease, which is characterized by cardiac conduction system dysfunction and gastrointestinal denervation, leading to esophageal and/or colonic dysfunction (manifesting as megaesophagus and megacolon). Acute Chagas disease is often diagnosed through peripheral blood smear, where the T. cruzi parasite can be visually identified. In contrast, diagnosing chronic Chagas disease is more challenging and typically requires serial serological or PCR testing. The only antimicrobial therapies with proven efficacy against T. cruzi infection are benznidazole and nifurtimox. Neither drug is FDA-approved but can be accessed under investigational protocols. These medications are used to treat congenital infections, acute infections, and chronic infections in younger patients (typically under 50 to 55 years of age), including those with early cardiomyopathy. Chronic Chagas disease frequently leads to congestive heart failure. Patients with Chagas cardiomyopathy often present with right bundle branch block and/or other arrhythmias. The affected hearts are typically dilated and hypertrophied, with areas of fibrosis, particularly at the apex, and may contain mural thrombi. Histologically, the myocardium shows infiltration by lymphocytes and macrophages, along with interstitial edema and fibrosis. The inflammatory reaction is most severe around the right bundle branch. Additionally, patients may develop megaesophagus and/or megacolon due to gastrointestinal involvement. The discovery of T. cruzi, the causative agent of Chagas disease, dates back to pre-Columbian times in South America. Carlos Chagas, a Brazilian bacteriologist, was the first to identify the association between the triatomine insect and T. cruzi. He named the pathogen in honor of his mentor, Oswaldo Cruz. Benznidazole, the first antimicrobial agent effective against T. cruzi infections, was introduced in 1966. The hallmark of Chagas disease is inflammation. During the acute phase, parasitemia occurs, characterized by parasitic replication and host immune responses, which contribute to the development of clinical manifestations. In the chronic phase, persistent low-grade inflammation is thought to lead to multisystem involvement. The pathogenesis of chronic Chagas disease is not fully understood but may involve either persistent parasites that evade elimination during the acute phase or autoimmune-mediated tissue destruction. Gross pathology in acute Chagas disease reveals inflammation, while chronic disease is marked by tissue dilation, congestion, fibrosis, and wall thickening. Microscopically, acute disease shows mononuclear and lymphocytic infiltration in infected tissues, which chronically results in tissue denervation and fibrous scar formation. Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy (CCM) is the most common chronic manifestation of the disease, accounting for 80% to 90% of chronic cases. Histologically, CCM is characterized by diffuse and patchy chronic myocarditis, interstitial mononuclear cell infiltrates, myocardial fiber destruction, and fibrotic replacement. Grossly enlarged hearts are often observed in autopsy studies of patients with end-stage Chagas disease, and left ventricular apical aneurysms are frequently identified. Chagas disease is caused by the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma cruzi. It must be differentiated from other diseases that cause cardiomyopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or esophageal/colonic dysfunction, such as electrophysiological cardiac diseases, gastrointestinal hypomotility disorders, and malignancies. The global incidence of Chagas disease is highest in South America, where it is endemic. Individuals of all age groups, including neonates, are at risk of acquiring the disease, particularly through vertical transmission. Elderly patients often present with clinical manifestations of chronic Chagas disease. While there is no evidence of racial predisposition, the majority of cases occur among individuals of Hispanic origin due to the endemicity of the disease in South America. Outside of South America, most cases are reported among South American immigrants. Risk factors for Chagas disease include residence in Central or South America, living in old houses with mud-and-stick walls or straw roofs, ingestion of contaminated water, and receiving blood transfusions or organ donations from individuals in endemic regions. Neonates are at higher risk if breastfed by infected mothers with bleeding or cracked nipples or if born to seropositive mothers with active disease. The acute phase of Chagas disease typically has an incubation period of 1 to 2 weeks. Most infected individuals remain asymptomatic during this phase. However, patients often remain chronically infected, with clinical manifestations appearing years or decades later. Chronic Chagas disease is most commonly associated with cardiomyopathy, which accounts for 80% to 90% of chronic cases. The majority of patients with Chagas cardiomyopathy die within two years of symptom onset. In the acute phase, symptoms are often nonspecific, such as fever, myalgia, fatigue, and anorexia. Less commonly, patients may present with severe disease suggestive of early Chagas myocarditis or meningoencephalitis. Chronic symptoms are generally related to either cardiomyopathy or gastrointestinal disease. On physical examination, findings may include fever, tachycardia, cardiac rhythm abnormalities, hepatosplenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy. A classic sign of Chagas disease, known as Romaña's sign, is characterized by eyelid swelling at the site of parasitic entry. Other physical findings are typically due to cardiac or gastrointestinal manifestations. Acute Chagas disease is often diagnosed through peripheral blood smear, where T. cruzi parasites can be visually detected. Serology is helpful for chronic cases, with diagnostic positivity requiring assays for both whole parasite lysate and recombinant antigen. However, the sensitivity and specificity of serological tests in chronic cases depend on the pre-test probability. On electrocardiography, right bundle branch block (RBBB) and atrioventricular (AV) block are common findings in patients with Chagas cardiomyopathy. Treatment options include benznidazole and nifurtimox, which are the only antimicrobial therapies with proven efficacy against T. cruzi. These drugs are not FDA-approved but can be accessed under investigational protocols. They are used to treat congenital infections, acute infections, and chronic infections in younger patients (under 50 to 55 years of age), including those with early cardiomyopathy. Primary prevention of Chagas disease involves the use of insecticides to control the vector, improved construction materials for walls and roofs, and testing of blood and organ donations prior to use.
